paras: The threatened lynching of James Beran took place in March 1903 at North Royalton, Ohio, where a crowd of villagers gathered at the place Beran was held on a charge of assaulting a school teacher, Gertrude Money. Officers took Beran out through a rear door and lodged him in the county jail at Cleveland on March 18, and no harm to him was reported. A single Cleveland dispatch carried the story to newspapers across the country the next day under headlines such as "Lynching Feared in Ohio" and "Ohio Mob Seeks Revenge."

According to the dispatch, Beran was from North Royalton and was charged with having "criminally assaulted" Money, a school teacher in the village, on Monday evening, March 16, while she was on her way home from school. The dispatch called the alleged attack "the crime" and said it created "intense excitement" in the village.

After the alleged assault, "the entire male population of the place turned out to hunt down the girl's assailant." Beran was found and locked up on the night of March 17. A crowd of citizens then gathered and, in the dispatch's words, "became so threatening" that officers took him out through a rear door and hurried him to the county jail in Cleveland.

He was lodged there on March 18, a move the Omaha Bee's copy attributed to "a strong sentiment among the people of that village to lynch him." None of the reports describes an attack on the place he was held or any injury to Beran, and none gives the size of the crowd.

Money was said to be in a serious condition when the dispatch was sent. No report of an indictment, trial or other outcome of the charge against Beran was found, and the coverage does not mention any action against the crowd.

The episode is known only from one Cleveland dispatch dated March 18, which ran on March 19 in the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier, the Omaha Bee, the Indianapolis Journal and the Wheeling Register. The same text appeared that day in the Salt Lake Herald, the Washington Evening Star, the Montgomery Advertiser, the Wichita Daily Eagle and the Portland Daily Press. No coverage in the Black press or in an Ohio paper was found, so every detail rests on the wire text.

Headline writers framed the identical text in different ways. The New Haven paper used "Lynching Feared in Ohio" over the deck "A Negro Charged With Assaulting a School Teacher," the only copy found that names Beran's race. Other desks put the crowd first, as in the Omaha Bee's "Ohio Mob Seeks Revenge" and the Portland Daily Press's "Enraged Citizens of Ohio Threaten to Lynch a Man," or the rescue, as in the Salt Lake Herald's "Saved From a Mob."

Some headlines hedged the charge, with the Indianapolis Journal calling Beran Money's "Alleged Assailant" and the Evening Star writing "Threats to Lynch Alleged Rapist." The Wheeling Register instead stated it as fact, heading the story "Beran, Who Assaulted School Teacher, Barely Escapes Lynching." In every copy the body text referred to "the crime" and "the girl's assailant," treating the accusation as settled while reporting the lynching threat without comment. Copies varied in small ways: several said "assaulted" rather than "criminally assaulted," the Salt Lake Herald dropped the manhunt and the crowd, and the Montgomery Advertiser spelled the name "Berren."

reader.title: Threatened lynching of James Beran
bases: A village crowd hunted Beran and then gathered threateningly where he was held, so officers removed him to Cleveland because a lynching was feared; no violence was done (A1, A2).
The dispatch reports a threatening crowd and fear of lynching but no killing; Beran was lodged safely in the Cleveland county jail (A1, A2).
Every copy found (A1-A9) is the same Cleveland wire dispatch of March 18; no local or independent report was found.

accounts.label: Cleveland wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Beran, charged with assaulting a teacher, was found after a village-wide hunt and locked up; a threatening crowd gathered and officers spirited him out a rear door to the Cleveland county jail because the village wanted to lynch him.

framing.detail: All copies reprint one Cleveland dispatch that treats the assault as 'the crime' and Beran as 'the girl's assailant'; headlines vary from 'Lynching Feared in Ohio' and 'Saved From a Mob' to 'Ohio Mob Seeks Revenge'.
Some desks hedged ('Alleged Assailant', 'Alleged Rapist', 'Man Accused of the Crime') while the Wheeling Register stated it as fact ('Who Assaulted School Teacher').

conflicts.note: Wording variants of one wire text, not independent accounts.
Spelling or OCR variants; most copies read Beran.
Only the New Haven desk's deck names a race; the wire text itself does not.

record_check.dossier: Alleged assault Monday evening, March 16; Beran found and locked up the night of March 17 (crowd gathered then); lodged in the Cleveland jail March 18. 03-17 is defensible for the crowd but the alleged assault was 03-16.
threatened: a crowd 'became so threatening' and lynching was feared, but no attack on the lockup or seizure attempt is described
pursuit (manhunt) is supported; 'siege' is not described, only a threatening crowd and secret removal through a rear door
'A Negro' in the New Haven deck only; the wire text and eight other copies name no race

record_check.record: accused of criminally assaulting a school teacher
record_check.dossier: supported; the teacher is named as Miss Gertrude Money
no county named in the papers; they say only North Royalton, Ohio, and the county jail in Cleveland
the same wire ran in at least nine papers on 1903-03-19; no Black-press coverage found
